hints: Recall which groups join to make a peptide link, the $\text{COOH}$ of the first amino acid and the $\text{NH}$ of the second, with loss of water.
Think about how proline is unusual, its N is in a ring with no extra H, so the Pro-Gly link is $\text{N-CO}$ with the Gly part as $\text{NH-CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$.
walkthrough:
Place Pro first, Gly second**
You are making Pro-Gly, so the carboxylic acid of proline joins to the amine of glycine. Keep the five membered proline ring intact with its N connected forward. Glycine is the simplest amino acid, just $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$, so after linking it becomes $\text{-NH-CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$.

Display the peptide link correctly**
Remove $\text{OH}$ from Pro $\text{COOH}$ and H from Gly $\text{NH}_{2}$ to give $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$. The question demands this link fully displayed, so draw $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ with all atoms and bonds shown, not as abbreviations.
Final answer: Pro ring-$\text{N-CO-NH-CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$ with peptide bond $\text{-CO-NH-}$ fully displayed. Pro $\text{COOH}$ carbon joined to Gly N, Gly shown as $\text{NH-CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$.

hints: Remember what small molecule is lost when $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NH}_{2}$ join to form $\text{CONH}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the small molecule lost**
Joining $\text{COOH}$ to an amine to give an amide always expels $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Any reaction that joins two molecules with loss of water is called condensation.

hints: Recall what holds alpha helices and beta sheets together, hydrogen bonds between $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{H-N}$ of peptide links.
walkthrough:
Check for the H-bond donor**
Normal secondary structure is stabilised by $\text{N-H}...\text{O=C}$ hydrogen bonds between chains. In poly(proline) every N is the ring N of proline, already bonded to two carbons plus the carbonyl carbon. With no $\text{N-H}$ left, it cannot donate a hydrogen bond.
Final answer: There is no H attached to N in the poly(proline) amide links, so no $\text{N-H}$ hydrogen bond donor is available.

hints: Decide whether $\text{NaOH}$ will react with the $\text{COOH}$ group or the amine group in proline.
walkthrough:
React the acid, leave the amine**
Dilute $\text{NaOH}$ neutralises the carboxylic acid to the sodium carboxylate plus water. The secondary amine ring is basic but with $\text{NaOH}$ there is no reaction there, so Q is the sodium salt of proline.
Final answer: $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{7}\text{NHCO}_{2}\text{H} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{7}\text{NHCO}_{2}\text{Na} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

hints: Use the dimethylamine example, the $\text{N-H}$ is replaced by $\text{N-COR}$ where $\text{R}$ comes from $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$.
walkthrough:
Acylate the ring nitrogen**
Just like $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{NH} + \text{RCOCl} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{NCOR} + \text{HCl}$, the proline $\text{NH}$ attacks $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$. Replace the $\text{N-H}$ by $\text{N-COCH}_{3}$. The $\text{COOH}$ stays unchanged, giving $\text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{3}$.
Final answer: N-acetyl proline: proline ring N bonded to $\text{COCH}_{3}$, structure $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{7}\text{N}(\text{COCH}_{3})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, shown as skeletal structure.

hints: Compare proline $\text{COOH}$ with prolinol $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, what type of change is loss of oxygen.
walkthrough:
Recognise acid to primary alcohol**
$\text{COOH}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ is a reduction needing a strong reducing agent that can reduce carboxylic acids. That classic reagent is lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$.

hints: Look at $\text{CH}_{2}(\text{CO}_{2}\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5})_{2}$ and identify the $\text{-COO-}$ linkage derived from a carboxylic acid and alcohol.
Look at $\text{CH}_{2}\text{=CHCN}$ and split it into the $\text{C=C}$ part and the $\text{-C}$ triple bond N part.
walkthrough:
Classify the diester**
$\text{-CO}_{2}\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ is $\text{-CO-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, the classic ester group. With two of them, the molecule is a diester.

Classify the two groups in acrylonitrile**
$\text{CH}_{2}\text{=CH-}$ contains a $\text{C=C}$ double bond, so alkene. $\text{-CN}$ contains $\text{C}$ triple bond N, so nitrile, also called cyanide.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{2}(\text{CO}_{2}\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5})_{2}$: ester. $\text{CH}_{2}\text{=CHCN}$: alkene and nitrile.

hints: Check whether any small molecule is lost when the two reactants combine to give U, or whether they simply add together.
walkthrough:
See two molecules become one**
U contains all the atoms of both reactants joined across the $\text{C=C}$ bond. Nothing is expelled, so this is an addition reaction.

hints: Focus on what changes from U to W, $\text{-CN}$ becomes $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$, which needs addition of hydrogen.
walkthrough:
Reduce the nitrile only**
Converting $\text{-C}$ triple bond N to $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ is reduction by hydrogen with a nickel, platinum or palladium catalyst. The esters are untouched under these conditions.
Final answer: $\text{H}_{2}$ / Ni or $\text{H}_{2}$ / Pt or $\text{H}_{2}$ / Pd

hints: Look at W forming a cyclic amide in X, the $\text{NH}_{2}$ attacks an ester carbonyl and displaces a small alcohol.
walkthrough:
Spot ring closure with loss of alcohol**
The amine end of W attacks one ester carbonyl intramolecularly to close a six membered lactam, expelling ethanol. Forming an amide from amine plus ester with loss of alcohol is classed as condensation, nucleophilic substitution at the carbonyl carbon.
Final answer: condensation or nucleophilic substitution or elimination

hints: When an ester $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ is attacked by an amine, what $\text{C}_{2}$ alcohol leaves.
walkthrough:
Identify Y from atom balance**
W to X plus Y loses the ethoxy part of one ester as $\text{-OCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ picks up H from the amine. That product is ethanol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.
Final answer: ethanol, $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$

hints: Start by identifying the nucleophile, the lone pair on $\text{NH}_{2}$, and the electrophile, the $\delta+$ carbon of the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond.
Recall how to show a nucleophilic substitution step with two curly arrows, one from the nucleophile to carbon and one from the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to Cl.
Think about what charge the nitrogen carries immediately after it forms the new bond but before it loses a proton.
walkthrough:
Set up nucleophile and electrophile**
Draw the lone pair on the $\text{NH}_{2}$ nitrogen clearly. Label the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond with partial charges, $\delta+$ on carbon and $\delta-$ on chlorine, because Cl is more electronegative and pulls electron density away.

Push the two curly arrows**
Draw one curly arrow starting at the nitrogen lone pair and pointing to the $\delta+$ carbon. Draw a second curly arrow starting in the middle of the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond and pointing to Cl, showing Cl leaving as $\text{Cl}^{-}$. This closes the five membered ring.

Draw the intermediate ion**
As soon as N forms the extra bond it becomes positively charged, $\text{NH}_{2}^{+}$ in the ring. Show this cyclic ammonium intermediate with the $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ still attached, which then loses $\text{H}^{+}$ to give neutral proline.

Final answer: Lone pair on $\text{NH}_{2}$ attacks $\delta+$ C of $\text{C-Cl}$ ($\delta-$ on Cl shown); curly arrow $\text{N:}$ to C and curly arrow $\text{C-Cl}$ to Cl; intermediate is cyclic ammonium ion with $\text{NH}_{2}^{+}$ closed to five membered ring bearing $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.

hints: Look for the carbon bonded to four different groups, the ring in two directions, H, and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.
walkthrough:
Find the carbon with four different attachments**
In proline only the alpha carbon carrying $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ is attached to four different groups: H, $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, N of the ring, and $\text{CH}_{2}$ of the ring. Mark this $\text{CH}$ with *.
Final answer: Asterisk on the $\text{*CHCO}_{2}\text{H}$ carbon, the alpha carbon attached to N, $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, H and $\text{CH}_{2}$.

hints: Count each $\text{-CO-NH-CH-}$ or $\text{-CO-N-}$ unit, including the terminal fragments, in the gelatin section shown.
walkthrough:
Count residue by residue**
Each amino acid contributes one carbonyl plus one alpha carbon in the chain. Working left to right through the diagram, including the partial residues at the ends, there are 9 distinct amino acid units.

hints: Recall that in water the acidic $\text{COOH}$ can donate a proton to the basic amine in the same molecule.
Think about what charges result, $\text{COO}^{-}$ and $\text{NH}_{2}^{+}$, and how to draw the proline ring with those charges.
walkthrough:
Draw the charged form**
Keep the five membered ring but change $\text{NH}$ to $\text{NH}_{2}^{+}$ and $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{COO}^{-}$. The molecule is overall neutral but has both positive and negative charges.

Explain the internal acid base reaction**
The $\text{COOH}$ group is acidic and the secondary amine is basic. A proton moves intramolecularly from $\text{COOH}$ to the nitrogen lone pair, giving $\text{COO}^{-}$ and $\text{NH}_{2}^{+}$.
Final answer: Zwitterion: proline ring with $\text{NH}_{2}^{+}$ and $\text{COO}^{-}$. Formed by transfer of $\text{H}^{+}$ from the carboxylic acid group to the amine group.

hints: Compare buffer pH 4.0 with each isoelectric point to decide if each amino acid is protonated (positive) or deprotonated (negative).
Recall that positive ions move toward the negative electrode and negative ions move toward the positive electrode.
For proline and alanine, both are below their isoelectric points at pH 4.0, so consider what common charge they carry.
For two ions with the same charge, consider how relative size or $M_{r}$ affects how far they migrate.
walkthrough:
Use pH versus pI to find the charge**
If pH is below pI the molecule is protonated and positive, if pH is above pI it is deprotonated and negative. At pH 4.0, glutamic acid with pI 3.1 is above its pI, so negative. Proline pI 6.5 and alanine pI 6.0 are below their pI values, so positive.

Predict direction of movement**
Negative glutamate is attracted to the positive pole, so its spot appears on the + side of the origin. Positive proline and alanine are attracted to the negative pole, so their spots appear on the - side.

Separate proline from alanine by size**
Both move the same way with the same +1 charge type, but mobility also depends on size. Alanine is much smaller with lower $M_{r}$ than the cyclic proline, so it experiences less friction and migrates farther from the origin toward the - end.

Label the electropherogram**
Draw three spots: one Glu spot to the left toward +, and two spots to the right toward -, with Ala farther from the centre X than Pro.

Final answer: Glutamic acid moves toward + electrode; proline and alanine move toward - electrode. At pH 4.0, Glu (pI 3.1) is negatively charged as $\text{COO}^{-}$ present, Pro and Ala (pI 6.5, 6.0) are positively charged as $\text{NH}_{2}^{+}$ / $\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ present. Alanine moves farther than proline toward - because it has lower $M_{r}$ / smaller size.

hints: Start by calculating initial moles of $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}\text{SNa}$ from mass over $M_{r}$ and moles of $\text{HCl}$ from concentration times volume.
Use the 1:1 reaction of salt with $\text{HCl}$ to find equilibrium moles of conjugate base left and weak acid ACES formed.
Convert $pK_{a}$ to $K_{a}$ with $K_{a}=10^{-pK_{a}}$ and set up $[\text{H}^{+}]=K_{a} \times [\text{acid}]/[\text{salt}]$.
Remember the final volume cancels in the ratio, but take $-\log[\text{H}^{+}]$ carefully to 2 decimal places for pH.
walkthrough:
Calculate starting moles**
Use $n=m/M_{r}$ for the salt:
$$n(\text{salt})=\frac{3.50}{204.1}=0.01715\text{ mol}$$
Use $n=cV$ for the acid, converting $\text{cm}^{3}$ to $\text{dm}^{3}$:
$$n(\text{HCl})=0.200 \times \frac{50.0}{1000}=0.0100\text{ mol}$$

Apply 1:1 stoichiometry to get buffer composition**
Salt + $\text{HCl} \rightarrow$ ACES + $\text{NaCl}$. All $\text{HCl}$ is consumed:
$$n(\text{base left})=0.01715-0.0100=0.00715\text{ mol}$$
$$n(\text{ACES formed})=0.0100\text{ mol}$$
Volume is common at $0.250$ $\text{dm}^{3}$, so the mole ratio equals the concentration ratio.

Find $K_{a}$ and $[\text{H}^{+}]$**
$$K_{a}=10^{-pK_{a}}=10^{-6.88}=1.32 \times 10^{-7}\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
For a buffer:
$$[\text{H}^{+}]=K_{a}\times\frac{[\text{acid}]}{[\text{salt}]}=1.32 \times 10^{-7}\times\frac{0.0100}{0.00715}=1.85 \times 10^{-7}\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

Convert to pH**
$$\text{pH}=-\log_{10}[\text{H}^{+}]=-\log_{10}(1.85 \times 10^{-7})=6.73$$
Give pH to 2 decimal places, consistent with the $pK_{a}$ data.

Final answer: Moles salt $=3.50/204.1=0.01715$ mol; moles $\text{HCl}=0.200 \times 50.0/1000=0.0100$ mol. Equilibrium moles base $=0.00715$ mol, moles ACES $=0.0100$ mol. $K_{a}=10^{-6.88}=1.32 \times 10^{-7}$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$; $[\text{H}^{+}]=1.32 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.0100/0.00715=1.85 \times 10^{-7}$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$; $\text{pH}=6.73$.
